newsitem.title: USA: Tax panel says Clinton budget raises taxes in 2002.
newsitem.headline: Tax panel says Clinton budget raises taxes in 2002.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's budget would result in a $13 billion tax increase after key tax cuts expire at the end of 2000, a congressional report said on Thursday.

The Joint Committee on Taxation, a Republican-dominated congressional panel that evaluates tax provisions, said Clinton's plan would yield the tax increase in 2002, the year targeted by lawmakers and the White House for reaching a balanced budget. This would come after four years of a tax cut totalling about $31.5 billion.

"I regret to report that the bottom line is bad news for the American people," said Representative Bill Archer, House Ways and Means Committee chairman. "The budget provides virtually no tax relief from now through 2002," the Texas Republican said.

The White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB) said it did not dispute the Joint Committee's report, but rather the reasons behind the finding were technical due to the administration's desire to have the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) say Clinton's budget wiped out the deficit.

The OMB sent legislative language to the CBO that would terminate tax cuts at the end of 2000 and cut spending 2.25 percent in fiscal 2001 and 2002, so that the CBO would find the president's budget balanced in 2002, OMB spokesman Larry Haas said.

The crux of the issue is that the CBO estimates the economy will grow more slowly in the next five years than does Clinton's budget office. To reach balance using the congressional analysts' methods, greater spending cuts and smaller tax cuts are required.

The Joint Committee found that proposed tax credits for families with young children, college tuition, individual retirement accounts, education and job training and environmental cleanup expenses would terminate at the end of 2000.

"This budget very artfully tries to have it both ways," Archer said. "The administration wants to say it has a balanced budget, while indicating to the American people that they will receive tax relief."
"I hope the president will agree to take a second look at his proposal," Archer added.

Clinton has proposed $98 billion in tax cuts over five years, while Senate Republicans have proposed nearly double that amount. Using OMB's estimates, Clinton's budget would result in a $5 billion net tax cut in fiscal 2002, Haas said.
